title: Clustering with k-means: finding groups without labels
summary: Group unlabelled examples by alternating two steps: assign each point to its nearest centre, then move each centre to its points' mean.
license: Original work for Python Intelligence; license to be chosen by the owner

steps.title: Groups nobody labelled
steps.body:
A shop has thousands of customers and no labels saying which are bargain hunters and which are big
spenders. A biologist has measurements of plants but no species names. **Clustering** looks for groups
of examples that are close to each other, using no labels at all. It is the first **unsupervised**
method in this course: there is no right answer to check predictions against.

steps.title: Two steps, repeated
steps.body:
Pick `k` starting centres. Then repeat two steps. **Assign:** give every point to its nearest centre.
**Update:** move every centre to the average of the points it was given. Each round, centres drift
towards the middle of a group, and points switch to the centre that now suits them better. When no
point switches, the groups are stable. This alternation, guess the groups, then refit the centres,
is the same idea as the EM algorithm for Gaussian mixtures, with each point given wholly to one
cluster instead of shared between them.

questions: If two starting centres sit right next to each other inside one group, what might happen to the other groups?
Why would measuring height in millimetres instead of metres change which points are 'nearest'?

steps.title: The precise rules
steps.body:
**Input:** examples `x₁ … x_N` (rows of `X`) and `k` starting centroids `μ₁ … μ_k`.

**Assign:** each example gets the label `j` of its nearest centroid in Euclidean distance (comparing
squared distances gives the same answer). This lesson breaks ties by choosing the lowest `j`.

**Update:** each centroid moves to the mean of the examples assigned to it. A centroid with no
examples stays where it is.

**Stop:** repeat assign-then-update until an iteration changes no assignment, or until `max_iter`
iterations have run.

**Inertia:** the sum of squared distances from each example to its own centroid. Each step can only
keep it the same or lower it, so k-means always stops, but at a *local* minimum: different starting
centroids can end in different, worse groupings. Larger `k` always allows lower inertia, so inertia
alone can't choose `k`.

**With NumPy:** `np.sum((C - x) ** 2, axis=1)` gives the squared distance from `x` to every row of
`C` by broadcasting; `np.argmin` returns the first position of the smallest value; `X[rows].mean(axis=0)`
averages selected rows.

steps.title: Run it: the start matters
steps.body:
Seven points on a line, three clusters, two different starting centres. Predict which start finds the
three obvious groups.

steps.title: Your turn: the assignment step
steps.body:
Complete `assign(X, centroids)`: return a list with, for each row of `X`, the position (an `int`) of
its nearest centroid in Euclidean distance; on a tie, the lowest position. Return `[]` when `X` has
no rows, and raise `ValueError` when there are no centroids. Don't change the inputs.
hints: For one row `x`, `np.sum((C - x) ** 2, axis=1)` holds its squared distance to every centroid.
`np.argmin` returns the first smallest position, which is exactly the tie rule; wrap it in `int(...)`.

import numpy as np

def assign(X, centroids):
    C = np.array(centroids, dtype=float)
    if C.ndim != 2 or len(C) == 0:
        raise ValueError('need at least one centroid')
    X = np.array(X, dtype=float).reshape(-1, C.shape[1])
    return [int(np.argmin(np.sum((C - x) ** 2, axis=1))) for x in X]

tests.name: ties go to the lowest position
tests.code:
assert assign([[5, 0]], [[0, 0], [10, 0]]) == [0], 'equally near: choose 0'
assert assign([[1, 1]], [[3, 1], [1, 3], [-1, 1]]) == [0], 'a three-way tie: choose 0'
assert assign([[0, 0]], [[9, 9], [1, 0], [0, 1]]) == [1], 'a tie between 1 and 2: choose 1'

tests.name: Euclidean distance
tests.code:
assert assign([[0, 0]], [[3, 3], [4.3, 0]]) == [0], 'straight-line distance: (3, 3) is about 4.24 away'
assert assign([[0, 0]], [[4.2, 0], [3, 3]]) == [0], 'straight-line distance: (4.2, 0) is nearer than (3, 3)'
assert assign([[0, 0]], [[4.242640587119285, 0], [3, 3]]) == [0] and assign([[0, 0]], [[3, 3], [4.242640787119286, 0]]) == [0], 'compare exact squared distances'

tests.name: near-ties are not ties
tests.code:
got = assign([[0.5000000001], [0.4999999999]], [[0], [1]])
assert got == [1, 0], f'just past halfway is nearer the second centroid: compare exact distances; got {got}'

tests.name: plain ints
tests.code:
got = assign([[0.5], [7]], [[0], [10]])
assert got == [0, 1] and type(got) is list and all(type(v) is int for v in got), 'a list of Python ints'

tests.name: no rows
tests.code: assert assign([], [[1, 2]]) == [], 'no rows in, no labels out'

tests.name: inputs are not changed
tests.code:
import copy
X, C = [[1.0, 2.0], [3.0, 4.0]], [[0.0, 0.0], [5.0, 5.0]]
keep = copy.deepcopy((X, C))
assign(X, C)
assert (X, C) == keep, 'do not modify X or centroids'

tests.name: no centroids

steps.solution:
import numpy as np

def assign(X, centroids):
    C = np.array(centroids, dtype=float)
    if C.ndim != 2 or len(C) == 0:
        raise ValueError('need at least one centroid')
    X = np.array(X, dtype=float).reshape(-1, C.shape[1])
    return [int(np.argmin(np.sum((C - x) ** 2, axis=1))) for x in X]

steps.title: Challenge: k-means from scratch
steps.body:
The starter gives you `assign`. Write `kmeans(X, init, max_iter=100)` following the rules above:
start from the centroids `init`, and each iteration assign every row, then move each centroid to the
mean of its rows (a centroid with none stays put). Stop after an iteration in which no assignment
changed, or after `max_iter` iterations. Return `{'centroids': [...], 'labels': [...], 'inertia': ...}`:
the centroids after the last update (lists of floats), the labels from the last assignment (ints),
and the inertia of those labels and centroids (a float). Raise `ValueError` if `X` or `init` is empty,
their widths differ, or `max_iter < 1`. Don't change `X` or `init`.
hints: Keep the previous labels in a variable; after updating the centroids, stop if the new labels equal it.
Copy the starting centroids with `np.array(init, dtype=float)` so updating them never changes `init`.

tests.name: two blobs
tests.code:
X = [[1, 1], [1.5, 2], [3, 4], [5, 7], [3.5, 5], [4.5, 5], [3.5, 4.5]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = kmeans(X, [[1, 1], [5, 7]])
assert got['labels'] == [0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1, 1], f'got {got["labels"]}'
assert close(got['centroids'][0], [1.25, 1.5]) and close(got['centroids'][1], [3.9, 5.1]), f'the means of each cluster; got {got["centroids"]}'
assert abs(got['inertia'] - 8.525) < 1e-9, f'sum of squared distances to the own centroid; got {got["inertia"]}'

tests.name: exactly one iteration
tests.code:
X = [[1, 1], [1.5, 2], [3, 4], [5, 7], [3.5, 5], [4.5, 5], [3.5, 4.5]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = kmeans(X, [[1, 1], [5, 7]], max_iter=1)
assert got['labels'] == [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 1], f'the first assignment puts (3, 4) with (1, 1); got {got["labels"]}'
assert close(got['centroids'][0], [11 / 6, 7 / 3]) and close(got['centroids'][1], [4.125, 5.375]), f'centroids after one update; got {got["centroids"]}'
assert abs(got['inertia'] - 12.208333333333332) < 1e-9, f'inertia of those labels and centroids; got {got["inertia"]}'

tests.name: the start matters
tests.code:
P = [[1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [10.0], [11.0], [12.0], [30.0]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
good = kmeans(P, [[1.0], [10.0], [30.0]])
bad = kmeans(P, [[1.0], [2.0], [3.0]])
assert good['labels'] == [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1, 2] and close([c[0] for c in good['centroids']], [2, 11, 30]) and abs(good['inertia'] - 4) < 1e-9, f'got {good}'
assert bad['labels'] == [0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2] and close([c[0] for c in bad['centroids']], [1, 2.5, 15.75]) and abs(bad['inertia'] - 273.25) < 1e-9, f'a poor start stops at a worse local minimum; got {bad}'

tests.name: an empty cluster stays put
tests.code:
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = kmeans([[0, 0], [1, 0], [0, 1]], [[0, 0], [50, 50]])
assert got['labels'] == [0, 0, 0] and close(got['centroids'][1], [50, 50]), f'no point is near (50, 50), so it keeps its place; got {got}'
assert close(got['centroids'][0], [1 / 3, 1 / 3]) and abs(got['inertia'] - 4 / 3) < 1e-9

tests.name: means, not medians
tests.code:
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = kmeans([[0], [1], [11], [100]], [[0], [100]])
assert got['labels'] == [0, 0, 0, 1] and close(got['centroids'][0], [4.0]), f'the mean of 0, 1 and 11 is 4; got {got}'

tests.name: max_iter limits the iterations
tests.code:
P = [[0.0], [1.0], [2.0], [3.0], [10.0], [11.0]]
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
two = kmeans(P, [[0.0], [1.0]], max_iter=2)
full = kmeans(P, [[0.0], [1.0]])
assert two['labels'] == [0, 0, 0, 1, 1, 1] and close([c[0] for c in two['centroids']], [1.0, 8.0]) and abs(two['inertia'] - 40) < 1e-9, f'after two iterations (not yet settled); got {two}'
assert full['labels'] == [0, 0, 0, 0, 1, 1] and close([c[0] for c in full['centroids']], [1.5, 10.5]) and abs(full['inertia'] - 5.5) < 1e-9, f'run to convergence; got {full}'

tests.name: ties inside k-means
tests.code:
close = lambda a, b: len(a) == len(b) and all(abs(x - y) < 1e-9 for x, y in zip(a, b))
got = kmeans([[5.0], [5.0]], [[0.0], [10.0]], max_iter=1)
assert got['labels'] == [0, 0] and close(got['centroids'][0], [5.0]) and close(got['centroids'][1], [10.0]), f'equally near both: choose 0; got {got}'

tests.name: plain lists of floats
tests.code:
X = [[1, 1], [1.5, 2], [3, 4], [5, 7], [3.5, 5], [4.5, 5], [3.5, 4.5]]
got = kmeans(X, [[1, 1], [5, 7]])
assert set(got) == {'centroids', 'labels', 'inertia'}, f'keys centroids, labels, inertia; got {sorted(got)}'
assert type(got['centroids']) is list and all(type(c) is list and all(isinstance(v, float) for v in c) for c in got['centroids'])
assert type(got['labels']) is list and all(type(v) is int for v in got['labels']) and isinstance(got['inertia'], float)

tests.name: inputs are not changed
tests.code:
import copy
import numpy as np
X, init = [[0.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.0], [9.0, 9.0]], [[0.0, 0.0], [9.0, 9.0]]
keep = copy.deepcopy((X, init))
kmeans(X, init)
assert (X, init) == keep, 'do not modify X or init'
A, B = np.array(X), np.array(init)
keepA, keepB = A.copy(), B.copy()
kmeans(A, B)
assert np.array_equal(A, keepA) and np.array_equal(B, keepB), 'not NumPy arrays either'

questions.prompt: Points 0, 2 and 10 are assigned to one centroid. Where does the update step move it?
What is the inertia of points 1 and 3 with a single centroid at 2?
Two runs of k-means with k = 3 on the same data end with inertia 40 and 25. Why can that happen?
choices: They started from different centroids and stopped at different local minima
One run must have a bug
questions.explanation: k-means only ever improves on where it started; different starts can settle in different groupings.

questions.prompt: Why can't you choose k simply by picking the k with the lowest inertia?
choices: Inertia keeps falling as k grows, down to 0 with one cluster per point
k must equal the number of features
questions.explanation: With one centroid on every point the inertia is 0, but those clusters mean nothing.

steps.title: What you can do now
steps.body:
- Explain clustering as finding groups in unlabelled data.
- Run k-means: assign each point to its nearest centroid, move each centroid to its points' mean, repeat.
- Measure a clustering with inertia, and know why it can't choose k by itself.
- Recognise that the starting centroids (and the units of the features) change the result.
